summary:
Curaçao stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, holding full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. The agreement commits the Kingdom's governments to equal treatment rather than establishing an immediately enforceable right for a visitor.

Official signals are mixed. Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly endorsed equal rights for everyone, and that endorsement ran against organised opposition from within her own party: Winifred Raveneau's fierce resistance had already forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel after a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement.

None of the sourcing addresses trans-specific provisions. Gender-marker and document rules, entry screening, restroom and facility access, healthcare restrictions and hate-crime protection are not documented for Curaçao in this inventory, so a trans visitor cannot rely on it to establish what they will face.
tangentialFactors:
Curaçao opened an LGBT 'Pink House' centre in 2010, and Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag has cited an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay-welcoming destination in the region. Both are community and tourism signals rather than legal protections.

Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. That is comparator context for the ABC islands, not Curaçao law, and it does not extend to Curaçao.

GlobalGayz, updated January 2017, profiles Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao as 'quiet nests of gay-friendliness' inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands and describes Curaçao, Sint Maarten and Aruba as drivers of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. This is a publication's own framing and carries no legal weight.
localsOnly:
Curaçao's residents have a functioning community infrastructure: an LGBT 'Pink House' centre has operated since 2010, and an annual Gay Pride is organised locally.

The 2013 Gay Pride had to be relocated to a hotel after a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement was imposed, an episode attributed to organised opposition from Pueblo Soberano's Winifred Raveneau. Public event permitting for LGBT gatherings has therefore been used as a political instrument.

Residents were the intended beneficiaries of the April 2015 Kingdom agreement and of the package of rights requests delivered to ministers in The Hague. The commitment runs to equal treatment by the Kingdom's governments rather than to an individually enforceable claim.

Party politics shape the local climate: commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone while facing resistance from inside her own party.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in the inventory covers trans-specific law in Curaçao. Rules on gender markers in passports and identity documents, airport or entry screening that could expose a visitor's trans status, facility and restroom access, restrictions or requirements affecting gender-affirming care, and hate-crime or hate-speech protection are all not sourced here.

Unresolved: whether the April 2015 Kingdom agreement on equal rights has been translated into binding legislation or policy in Curaçao is not documented. The agreement commits the Kingdom's governments to equal treatment; it does not itself create a right a visitor could enforce.

Not sourced: no evidence in this inventory addresses violence against trans people in Curaçao, whether any complaints mechanism exists, or how police handle identity-document discrepancies. The absence of such material should not be read as an absence of risk.
